title: Suno Faces Lawsuits from Elvis Estate and Eminem Publisher Over AI Infringement
summary: Elvis Presley’s estate and Eminem’s publisher have sued AI music generator Suno, alleging copyright and likeness violations.

 Suno Faces Lawsuits from Elvis Estate and Eminem Publisher Over AI Infringement
 Ongoing 
 By Deimos EMK · Published Nov 7, 2026 · 2 min read · Sourced & fact-checked 
 Photo: Brendan_linden (cc0), via Wikimedia Commons | Via YouTube channel @Elvis Presley All clips and posts below are embedded from their original sources.
 By the numbers: this timeline documents 7 events from Nov 6, 2026 to Nov 7, 2026, drawn from 4 sources.
 “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work,”
 via variety.com 
 Our take
 These suits underscore the growing tension between AI developers and artists’ rights holders. By invoking the ELVIS Act, the Presley estate is testing whether AI companies can be held liable for cloning a performer’s voice. The outcome could set precedent for how future AI music platforms must navigate copyright and likeness laws.
 Background
 Elvis Presley’s estate, managed by Authentic Brands Group, controls the singer’s catalog and likeness rights. In October 2026, the estate sued Anthropic for training its Claude model on Elvis songs.
 Eight Mile Style, a Detroit-based publisher that administers many of Eminem’s hits, has sued Suno alleging the platform used the rapper’s copyrighted works to train its AI, according to giantswire.usatoday.com.

The lawsuits and Suno's denial are documented only through coverage by Billboard, USA Today, Variety, and Vice, while the actual court documents and direct party statements remain unverified. The legal proceedings are pending and no rulings have been reported.

Elvis Music Owners, Eminem Publisher File Sprawling New Lawsuits Against AI Music Generator Suno: ‘The Next Elvis Won’t Pick Up a Guitar’
 By 
 Corbin Bolies 
 Plus Icon

 A collection of Elvis Presley music rightsholders and the publisher of many of Eminem ‘s records have filed sprawling new federal lawsuits against the AI music generator Suno , with each party making separate allegations that add to the AI company’s legal challenges.
 The Presley lawsuit — brought by a group that includes Authentic Brands Group, Raleigh Music Publishing and others against the AI music generator in the Northern District of California — accuses the platform of copyright infringement and exploiting Presley’s identity whenever Suno users cite his name when they generate new songs. They claimed in a 51-page filing that Suno violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security — or, ELVIS — Act, a 2024 law that prevents AI companies from cloning singers’ voice, by allowing users to generate tracks that mirror Presley’s “rich vocal timbre” without permission.
 Related Stories 
 Raye to Headline BST Hyde Park With Sienna Spiro Opening 
 Raye Named Variety’s 2026 Hitmaker of the Year 
 Eight Mile Style, an LLC that controls hundreds of Eminem recordings, including “Lose Yourself,” “Without Me” and “The Real Slim Shady,” alleged in its own case that Suno infringed upon its copyright by allowing users to generate songs and lyrics that mirror the rapper’s tracks. Eminem is not individually participating in the suit, and a representative for the rapper did not respond to an immediate request for comment.
 Attorneys Richard Busch, Mark Block, David Niemierzycki and Andrew Davis — who are representing both the Presley group and Eight Mile Style — argued that Suno has “mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of cold hard cash.” Both complaints included several examples of generated songs that either allegedly sounded like Presley or produced lyrics replicating Eminem’s work.
 “The next Elvis won’t pick up a guitar,” the attorneys wrote in the Presley case. “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect, begging the question from future generations who would attempt to start what is already an arduous, uncertain, and not always lucrative creative pursuit: ‘What’s the point?’”
 Elements of the Presley lawsuit mirror one brought by Americana singer Jason Isbell and other musicians , who alleged in a filing seeking class-action status that Suno’s platform allows users to exploit their identities. Suno has denied those allegations.
 “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work,” a Suno spokesperson said in a statement. “To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”
 The Presley case is the latest test of whether an artist or their estate can employ the legal system to protect their name, image and likeness from use by an AI company without explicit authorization or compensation, a fear induced by AI models and deepfakes since generative technology took hold of the public sphere. In the Isbell-led suit, the plaintiffs argued that Suno’s platform allowed users to bypass its restrictions by using specific prompts that, instead of using an artist’s name, asked for tracks that invoked their “tone and phrasing” by using real names instead of stage names (as in the case of the rapper Common) or by adding spaces between the letters of their names, among other methods.
 “This lawsuit seeks to recover the value of those misappropriated identities and to stop their ongoing commercial exploitation,” attorney Alan D. Rose wrote in that lawsuit. Suno denied the allegations and said in court there was “nothing unlawful” about asking for a song in the vein of an artist.

Elvis Presley Rights Owners Sue Suno Over AI Voice Cloning: ‘Elvis’ Identity Was Stolen’
 The singer's legendary voice is at the center of a cutting-edge lawsuit that aims to hold the AI firm legally liable for allowing users to create knockoff vocals.
 By
 Bill Donahue 
 Bill Donahue 
 View All

 Elvis Presley, 21, seen in April 1956. The owner's of Presley's intellectual property is suing the AI company Suno for allowing users to clone his voice. 
 Underwood Archives/Getty Images 
 Español 
 The owners of Elvis Presley ’s intellectual property are suing Suno in a new lawsuit that claims the artificial intelligence music company violated the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll’s likeness rights by stealing his voice.
 Weeks after suing AI giant Anthropic for training Claude on Elvis songs, the new case filed Friday (Nov. 6) by Elvis Presley Enterprises levels similar copyright accusations against Suno, the leading AI music firm. But it also includes legally-novel allegations that Suno broke the law by letting users clone Presley’s “unmistakable and iconic voice.”
 Related 
 Anthropic Sued For Stealing Elvis Presley Music to Train AI: ‘Deeply Protective of These Iconic Songs’ 
 Bill Donahue 
 “All of the humanity, history, despair, and triumph that constitutes Elvis’ identity was stolen and is stored on servers and harnessed by Suno to make massive amounts of money,” writes Richard Busch, a veteran music litigator at the firm Adams & Reese who filed the case. “Suno did so intentionally, maliciously, and fraudulently to financially benefit itself and artificially compete with Elvis’ likeness and copyrights, and continues to do so to this day.”
 The new lawsuit marks one of the first major cases under a new Tennessee law, coincidentally called the ELVIS Act, that was recently enacted to address problems caused by AI. The first-in-the-nation statute was touted as a weapon against people who create illegal deepfakes, but it also allows for lawsuits against tech firms that enable such voice and image cloning in the first place.
 Taken together with the Anthropic case, the suits over Elvis represent easily most significant action filed on behalf of an individual musician over AI — in this case, arguably the most famous recording artist of all time. Suno and Anthropic were already facing cases from music labels accusing them of infringing millions of copyrighted songs to train their models, as well as a class action by smaller artists who similarly say Suno stole their likenesses.
 Friday’s lawsuit was filed by Elvis Presley Enterprises, a unit of the licensing giant Authentic Brands Group that controls the intellectual property tied to Elvis, including much of his song catalog and the rights to his name, image and likeness. In a statement to Billboard on Saturday, ABG spokeswoman Lark-Marie Antón said the new lawsuit and its evidence “speak for themselves.”
 “The name, image, likeness, and music of Elvis Presley are among the most valuable intellectual property assets in the world,” Antón said. “We protect those rights vigorously.” 
 In statement Saturday responding to the lawsuit, a Suno spokeswoman told Billboard : “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”
 The looming battle with Suno will raise untested legal questions about the extent to which AI companies can be sued for allegedly ripping off a musical artist’s identity. The use of AI to convincingly mimic real people has been one of the booming technology’s most controversial applications, and no where less so than an industry largely built on famous singing voices.
 “Elvis’ voice possessed a distinctively rich vocal timbre, with a warm velvety resonance and perfectly employed vibrato, coupled with his ability to vary his technique and delivery within the same song as well as across several different styles of music, which became his immediately recognizable musical signature across the world,” the lawsuit says.
 Suno has argued in other lawsuits that its current models do not allow users to include the names of specific artists in prompts, nor produce outputs that mimic specific real voices.  Elvis Presley Estate Warns ‘The Next Elvis Won’t Pick up a Guitar’ in New Lawsuit Against AI Music Company Suno
 The Elvis Presley estate takes another AI company to court for alleged copyright infringement and violating a law that protects them from it.
 By Caleb Catlin 
 November 7, 2026, 1:19pm 
 Share: 
 Share on X (Opens in new window) X 
 Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook 
 Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard 
 Add Us On Google
 No one has been as protective against AI quite like the Elvis Presley estate. Back in October 2026, they took Anthropic to court for allegedly stealing 274 songs to train their AI without permission. One of the songs they utilized is one of the most iconic ballads of all time, “Can’t Help Falling in Love”. According to lead attorney Richard Busch, they built their company off the backs of artists “at a scale never seen before.”
 Now, in a new report from Variety , they’re taking another AI conglomerate to court. The Elvis Presley estate filed a litany of lawsuits against Suno for immense copyright infringement and exploiting the King of Rock ‘n’ Roll. Additionally, there’s a law in Tennessee that would effectively guarantee protection from companies like Suno cloning his voice.
 Videos by VICE 
 Ultimately, the attorneys behind the lawsuit warned that if these companies remain unchecked, they can copy any music legend at a troubling precedent. Then, the future of image and likeness would essentially be lost forever. 
 “The next Elvis won’t pick up a guitar,” they wrote. “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect, begging the question from future generations who would attempt to start what is already an arduous, uncertain, and not always lucrative creative pursuit: ‘What’s the point?’”
 Elvis Presley Estate Takes Suno to Court for Immense Copyright Infringement
 Meanwhile, Suno maintained that their AI tech training merely allowed the precedent for new, original music. Moreover, they insisted that they’ve never been against putting in the proper guardrails in order to maintain their progress. 
 “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness,” a spokesperson responded to the Elvis Presley estate. “We prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”
 The Elvis Presley estate isn’t the only group taking Suno to court either. Eight Mile Style, a publishing company with rights to many classic Eminem songs, also filed their own lawsuits. They argued a similar case, that Suno was using the Detroit MC’s tracks to mirror his style for new songs. However, Eminem himself won’t be involved in the case.
